title: Foundations of Nursing (NSC 201)
description: History and theories of nursing, the nursing process, infection prevention, basic nursing procedures and professional ethics.

topics.title: History and Theories of Nursing
topics.summary: Florence Nightingale, development of nursing in Nigeria, and major nursing theorists.

notes.b: Florence Nightingale is regarded as the founder of modern nursing. During the Crimean War (1854–1856) she reduced soldiers' death rates through sanitation and hygiene, and in 1860 founded the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital, London. Her 'Notes on Nursing' emphasised environment. International Nurses Day (12 May) is her birthday. In Nigeria, formal nurse training began in mission hospitals; the Nursing Council of Nigeria (now the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria) was established in 1947 and university nursing education began at the University of Ibadan in 1965.
k: Florence Nightingale: founder of modern nursing
University nursing in Nigeria began at UI (1965)

notes.b: Nightingale's Environmental Theory: manipulating the environment (ventilation, light, cleanliness, noise, nutrition) promotes healing. Virginia Henderson defined nursing as assisting the individual in activities contributing to health or recovery that they would perform unaided if they had the strength, will or knowledge (14 basic needs). Dorothea Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory: nursing is needed when self-care demands exceed abilities (wholly compensatory, partly compensatory, supportive-educative systems). Other theorists include Hildegard Peplau (interpersonal relations), Callista Roy (adaptation model) and Madeleine Leininger (transcultural nursing).

topics.title: The Nursing Process
topics.summary: Assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.

notes.b: The nursing process is a systematic, patient-centred problem-solving method with five steps (ADPIE): Assessment (collecting subjective and objective data by interview, observation and examination), Nursing diagnosis (clinical judgement about the patient's response to health problems, e.g. using NANDA-I labels such as 'Acute pain related to surgical incision as evidenced by…'), Planning (setting priorities and SMART goals, and choosing interventions), Implementation (carrying out the plan) and Evaluation (judging whether goals were met and revising the plan).
k: Subjective data: what the patient says; objective: what you observe/measure

notes.b: Priorities are often set using Maslow's hierarchy of needs (physiological needs first, then safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation) and the ABC approach (airway, breathing, circulation). A nursing diagnosis differs from a medical diagnosis: it describes the patient's response (e.g. 'impaired physical mobility') rather than the disease (e.g. 'fractured femur'). Documentation must be accurate, timely, legible, signed and factual — 'if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done'.
k: Nursing diagnosis = patient's response, not disease

topics.title: Infection Prevention and Control
topics.summary: Chain of infection, hand hygiene, standard precautions, PPE and waste management.

notes.h: Chain of infection and hand hygiene
notes.b: The chain of infection has six links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission (contact, droplet, airborne, vector, vehicle), portal of entry and susceptible host; breaking any link prevents infection. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent health-care-associated infections. WHO's 'My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene': before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings. Alcohol-based hand rub (20–30 seconds) is preferred unless hands are visibly soiled or after caring for patients with C. difficile diarrhoea (use soap and water, 40–60 seconds).
k: Six links in the chain of infection
Soap and water if visibly soiled

notes.b: Standard precautions apply to all patients: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection) based on risk, safe injection practices (never recap needles; dispose into a sharps container), respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning and safe handling of linen and waste. Transmission-based precautions add contact, droplet or airborne measures (N95 respirators for TB, measles). Health-care waste is segregated by colour coding: in Nigeria yellow for infectious waste, black for general non-infectious waste, and puncture-proof sharps boxes for needles. Needlestick injuries should be washed, reported and assessed for post-exposure prophylaxis.
k: Yellow bag: infectious waste; black: general

topics.title: Basic Nursing Procedures and Patient Comfort
topics.summary: Vital signs, positioning, pressure-ulcer prevention, hygiene and medication administration.

notes.b: Vital signs (temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, pain) are measured accurately and charted; early warning scores flag deterioration. Positions: Fowler's (semi-sitting, 45–60°) eases breathing; semi-Fowler's (30°); supine; prone; lateral; Sims' (semi-prone, for enemas and rectal examination); lithotomy (for pelvic examination and delivery); Trendelenburg (head down). Immobile patients should be turned at least every 2 hours to prevent pressure ulcers, which occur over bony prominences (sacrum, heels, hips). The Braden scale assesses pressure-ulcer risk.

Nurses follow the 'rights' of medication administration: right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time, right documentation (often extended to right reason and right response). Check allergies and identify the patient with two identifiers. Intramuscular sites include the deltoid (small volumes), ventrogluteal (preferred, safest for large volumes) and vastus lateralis (preferred in infants). Insulin and heparin are given subcutaneously. Never administer a drug prepared by someone else or an unlabelled drug.
k: Rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation
Ventrogluteal is the safest IM site for adults

topics.title: Professional Ethics, Law and Communication in Nursing
topics.summary: Ethical principles, patients' rights, consent, confidentiality, and therapeutic communication.

notes.b: The four principles of bioethics are autonomy (respecting the patient's right to decide), beneficence (doing good), non-maleficence (avoiding harm) and justice (fairness in care and resources). Informed consent must be voluntary, given by a competent person, and based on adequate information about the procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives. Confidentiality protects patient information; it may be breached only with consent, by law, or to protect others from serious harm. Negligence occurs when a duty of care is breached and causes harm. Nurses in Nigeria follow the NMCN Code of Professional Conduct and the ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses.

Therapeutic communication builds trust and supports care. Techniques include active listening, open-ended questions, silence, reflection, paraphrasing, clarification and summarising; barriers include false reassurance, giving advice prematurely, judgemental responses, medical jargon and language differences (use interpreters). Peplau described phases of the nurse–patient relationship: orientation, working (identification and exploitation) and termination/resolution. The SBAR tool (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) structures handover and communication with colleagues.
